source.title: Transferable Model-agnostic Vision-Language Model Adaptation for Efficient Weak-to-Strong Generalization
source.authors: Jihwan Park; Taehoon Song; Sanghyeok Lee; Miso Choi; Hyunwoo J. Kim

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplement are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests weak-to-strong adaptation transfer in vision, but uses a different intervention from the original: it transfers an adapter trained to capture the gap between a weak VLM's pretrained and fine-tuned predictions, rather than fine-tuning a strong student on labels produced by the weak model.
record.gate_note: The paper does not fine-tune the strong model on weak-model-produced labels and does not calculate PGR. Its results bear on V6: whether weak-to-strong adaptation transfer works in vision. It reports adapter-transfer results and comparisons with fine-tuned weak-model performance. TransMiter+ results that add labeled-data fine-tuning are not treated as evidence for the weak-label effect.
record.test_reason: Vision (CLIP-family VLMs) weak-to-strong transfer by a different method. An adapter is trained on unlabeled images to mimic the fine-tuned weak model's logits, then moved to a stronger pre-trained VLM by closed-form alignment. The paper reports strong-target accuracy against the fine-tuned weak source (supervisor), the strong zero-shot model and the strong fine-tuned ceiling, so PGR-like quantities can be computed. It also reports naive weak-teacher distillation baselines (Prompt Transfer, PromptKD), which are closer to the original recipe.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors add that TransMiter beats the other transfer baselines and preserves novel-class generalization. They also claim that TransMiter+ (with labeled data) often surpasses a fine-tuned stronger model.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an adapter trained to match fine-tuned weak-model predictions from unlabeled images, followed by closed-form feature alignment for a strong target; it does not fine-tune the strong model on weak-produced labels. The additional TransMiter+ stage uses labeled data.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with source-target model pairing and source fine-tuning strategy. The paper also reports settings varying task/dataset, base-to-base versus base-to-novel evaluation, shot count, pre-training objective, domain shift, and adapter components such as auxiliary classes and basis change.
record.problems: No PGR is reported, so the results do not quantify the proportion of a strong-versus-weak performance gap recovered. The main transfer mechanism is an adapter rather than weak-label fine-tuning. Accuracy is reported as an average over 3 seeds in the supplement, but no error bars or other uncertainty estimates are given. Some Table 1 aggregate values are difficult to assign from the flattened table; rows use values stated explicitly in the prose.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted per-dataset entries from Table 2, individual domain-shift variant scores in Table 10, and additional model/component ablations and comparisons in Tables 3–5, 11, 13–21. Priority was given to stated aggregate transfer outcomes and settings directly demonstrating vision transfer; TransMiter+ results involving subsequent labeled-data fine-tuning were not treated as evidence for weak-label transfer.

untested.parts: TransMiter does not fine-tune the strong model on weak labels. Only the naive-KD baselines (PromptKD, Prompt Transfer) approximate the recipe, and they are not rows.
The listed training changes (confidence loss, ensembling, loss variants) are not tested against naive weak-label fine-tuning.
Source/target size is varied (RN50, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14, ViT-H/14), but only for adapter transfer. PGR, task dependence and predictors are not analysed.
No tests of exploitation or shared errors. Domain shift (r14) is evaluated, but not as a failure-mode test.
No theory on when a student must beat its supervisor.
The original weak-label fine-tuning recipe in vision is tested only via the baselines; there are no direct rows for it.

missing.what: PromptKD (naive KD, weak ViT-B/16 teacher → ViT-L/14 student): base-to-base 78.75 vs source FT 81.74; base-to-novel 83.34/74.61/78.43 vs source 84.19/75.35/79.53. The student is below its supervisor.

Prompt Transfer (KD-adapted prompts) vs source FT in the Table 1 Avg column. RN50→ViT-B/16: 62.74 vs 73.39. RN50→ViT-L/14: 77.28 vs 73.39. ViT-B/16→ViT-L/14 CoOp: 78.50 vs 79.92. PromptSRC: 73.41 vs 81.74. Table 2 HM: 76.94 vs 79.53.
ViT-L/14→ViT-H/14 (DFN-5B). TransMiter base-to-base 87.15 vs source FT 85.17 and target zero-shot 82.12. Base-to-novel HM 89.15 vs source 84.28 and target zero-shot 87.37. EFT collapses to 56.63 HM.

record.verdict_notes: TransMiter is not strong-model fine-tuning on weak labels: an adapter learned on the weak model's logits is mapped onto the strong model's logits. Beating the supervisor is often driven by strong zero-shot ability; e.g. on ViT-H/14 and in novel/domain-shift settings, zero-shot already beats the supervisor. PGR-like values were computed by the verifier from Table 1/2 values, not reported by the paper. Prompt Transfer trains only a projection or prompts for one epoch, so its failure is weak evidence. PromptKD is closer to the original recipe. Results are 3-seed averages with no uncertainty reported. The Table 1 flattening misaligns some per-dataset columns; the Avg values are consistent with the prose.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train a strong student on labels produced by a weak supervisor or report PGR.
Ablates adapter components, but does not test the listed changes against naive weak-label fine-tuning using PGR.
Includes VLM size, architecture, and visual-task variations, but does not measure PGR or its dependence on those factors.
Does not test weak-supervisor blind spots, shared error patterns, or weak-label distribution-shift failure modes as defined in the claim.
No theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor are tested.
Tests vision-language model adaptation transfer with an adapter, not the original weak-label fine-tuning recipe or PGR.
